chapterOverview.guidingQuestion: What are the characteristic properties and behaviors of waves?
chapterOverview.purpose: Understand properties of wave pulses and simple waves and the behaviors observed when waves interact with each other or with their surroundings.
chapterOverview.centralIdeas: Waves transfer energy without permanently displacing matter. A wave pulse forms when a push or pull transfers energy to a medium; repeated pulses produce a simple wave with characteristic features. The wavelength—and therefore wave speed observed for a given source—depends on properties of the transmitting medium.

table.waveProps: Waves are caused by disturbances and travel away from the source.
table.waveBehav: Objects bob up and down but do not travel with the wave. Vibrating materials make sound; sound can make things move.

table.waveProps: Features of the disturbance influence amplitude and spacing between pulses.
table.waveBehav: Waves of the same type interact at the crossing point but continue unaffected afterward.

table.waveProps: Simple waves arise from repetitive disturbances.
table.waveBehav: Waves transmit energy through matter (e.g., water, sound, spring).

table.waveProps: Wave speed is determined by medium characteristics.
table.waveBehav: Waves reflect, refract, and transmit differently when crossing media; some frequencies cause materials to vibrate (resonance).

progression.narrative: The progression can use a consistent toolkit (e.g., shallow water pans and tuning forks). Early grades see ripples propagate away from a disturbance and connect vibrations to sound. Late elementary compares amplitudes and spacing and observes wave interference that is temporary at the crossing point. Middle school formalizes simple waves and models sound. High school quantifies the role of the medium in wave speed and investigates reflection, refraction, transmission, and resonance.

K-2.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 2, waves ... can be made in water by disturbing the surface ... Sound can make matter vibrate, and vibrating matter can make sound. – NRC, 2012
K-2.progression: Young children observe sound and water waves in daily life. They see that motion in one place causes motion elsewhere (a floating object bobs but does not travel with the wave). Repeating a splash produces repeating bobs that show waves carry patterns of motion. Clear setups reduce reflections to make patterns easier to see. Early experiences also link sound with vibration (e.g., tuning fork in water, cup-and-string phones).

3-5.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 5, waves of the same type can differ in amplitude and wavelength and can add or cancel one another as they cross ... Earthquakes cause seismic waves. – NRC, 2012
3-5.progression: Students learn air is a medium that can transmit motion like water. They explore how stronger disturbances make taller waves, and how steady sources produce evenly spaced pulses. They observe that when waves meet, effects are temporary at the crossing point; waves continue unchanged. Introduce seismic waves qualitatively as motion in Earth’s crust.

6-8.nrcQuote: By the end of grade 8, a simple wave has a repeating pattern with a specific wavelength, frequency, and amplitude. A sound wave needs a medium. – NRC, 2012
6-8.progression: Students model simple waves from repeating disturbances and represent sound as a pressure wave that needs a medium. Seismic waves illustrate how wave behavior reveals unseen structures.

standards.statement: Plan and conduct investigations to demonstrate the cause-and-effect relationship between vibrating materials and sound.
standards.bigIdea: Vibrating materials can cause sound, and sound can cause materials to vibrate.
scientificIdeas: Striking or disturbing an object can make it vibrate (back-and-forth motion).
Vibrations can be fast or slow and last different amounts of time.
Some vibrating materials produce sounds we can hear.
Stopping the vibration stops the sound.
Sound can cause objects to vibrate (e.g., rice on a drumhead).
Harder hits generally make louder sounds.
A tuning fork in water shows ripples that move outward, linking sound to distant motion.
studentIdeas: Some sounds happen without any vibration (e.g., snapping, crickets, TV).
Only musical instruments can make sound.
Sound can’t bend around obstacles or corners.
Covering the mouth traps sound so it cannot be heard.
Only hard hits create vibrations; quiet sounds don’t vibrate anything.
Vibrations only occur in solids, not in air or water.
If you can’t see or feel motion, nothing is vibrating.

standards.statement: Use a model of a simple wave to describe amplitude, wavelength, and explain how waves can add or cancel each other as they cross.
standards.bigIdea: Waves have measurable properties determined by how they are generated; simple representations can show amplitude, wavelength, and interference.
scientificIdeas: A force that disturbs a medium creates a pulse; repeated disturbances create a simple wave.
Stronger forces create greater displacement of the medium and taller waves.
Spacing between pulses depends on timing between disturbances.
Waves transfer energy away from the disturbance.
Medium particles return to original positions after the wave passes; they are not carried with the wave.
When waves overlap, they can add or cancel at the same place and time.
Opposite-phase crests/troughs of equal size can cancel completely; unequal sizes cancel partially.
Crest-crest or trough-trough overlap produces temporarily larger disturbance.
After crossing, simple waves continue without permanent change.
studentIdeas: Waves are objects that collide and bounce off each other.
Bigger waves permanently destroy smaller waves when they meet.
If two waves meet, they stop or block each other.
Waves always add to make a bigger wave.

standards.statement: Develop and use models to represent the basic properties of waves in a system including frequency, amplitude, wavelength, and speed.
standards.bigIdea: A simple wave is a repeating disturbance; its properties (frequency, amplitude, wavelength, speed) depend on the source and the medium.
scientificIdeas: Repeated disturbances form simple waves.
Waves transfer energy away from the source.
Stronger disturbances produce greater displacement (amplitude).
More frequent disturbances produce waves that are closer together (higher frequency, shorter wavelength for a fixed speed).
Different media transmit waves at different speeds.
For a given source and medium, longer wavelengths correspond to faster wave speed; within a fixed medium, speed is set by the medium and wavelength varies with frequency.
Sound is a simple wave that requires a medium and can be modeled as alternating compressions and rarefactions.
studentIdeas: Waves slow down the farther they travel through a medium, like objects do.
Frequency and speed are the same thing.
All waves move at the same speed regardless of medium.
Wave properties are unrelated to how the wave was created or the medium.
Changing frequency does not affect wavelength.
Some waves form without any energy input.
